<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but B's pressure sequence exposed a genuine structural dilemma in A's proposal that A never fully escaped. B forced A to define the trigger precisely, and A's answer ("any denial, cut, or termination of benefits, any deportation, detention, or adverse immigration determination, any decision lengthening criminal exposure") confirmed B's charge that the "narrow, serious-consequence" right actually swallows the entire caseload — directly undercutting A's Rebuttal 1 claim that the right was workable because narrow. B then landed a second decisive blow: A's own test for distinguishing genuine human review from rubber-stamping (individualized reasons, record engagement, documented departures, liability) is purely procedural and, as B pointed out, could be satisfied by a well-audited algorithm — meaning A's remedy is functionally identical to B's proposed alternative (explanation, appeal, audit) without requiring a human body at all. A's closing reasserted "only a human can take responsibility" but never directly answered why liability or mercy requires a human rather than an accountable institution or algorithm-plus-audit regime, leaving this central tension unresolved in A's favor. A had strong opening framing and made good counters on bias-correctability and delay costs, but ultimately did not repair the two core cracks B exposed. B's opening was clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost, but B's subsequent rounds more than compensated by sharpening the clash and forcing A into a dilemma it could not cleanly resolve.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 point [B4.2]–[B4.4]: showing that A's own "genuine reconsideration" test is procedural (not human-specific) and that A's trigger definition, once specified, covers the entire agency caseload — collapsing A's narrow/workable framing from Rebuttal 1.</best_rebuttal>
